The tested H-Darrieus turbine had a swept area of 1.5 m^2 and was equipped with dihedral blades composed of unstaggered NACA0021 profiles with a chord of 0.086 m.
The wind tunnel experiments were conducted in an open-jet configuration to minimize blockage effects, with a freestream turbulence intensity less than 1%.
The CFD simulations used a 2D unsteady RANS approach with the k-ω SST turbulence model, with a total of 1.2 million elements in the rotating region and 2.0 million elements in the stationary region.
The CFD simulations were corrected a posteriori to account for the resistant torque of the supporting spokes and the tip effects, which could not be directly included in the 2D simulations.
The authors found that the tip effects resulted in an equivalent blade span reduction of 1.5 chord lengths, which was in good agreement with the Leicester-Prandtl model.
At low tip-speed ratios (TSR = 1.5, 1.8), the wake showed strong localized regions of fluctuations and the presence of large vortices shed from the blades.
At higher TSR (2.4), the wake was more stable with a smoother velocity profile, and the periodic unsteadiness in the wake was significantly reduced.
The periodic unsteadiness, measured as the root-mean-square of the phase-resolved velocity component, was higher in the regions where the macrovortices were being detached from the blades.
The CFD simulations showed good agreement with the experimental data in terms of the power curve and the mean wake profiles, especially at lower tip-speed ratios.
Some discrepancies were observed in the unstable part of the power curve due to the challenges in accurately predicting the stall characteristics of the airfoils.

The authors acknowledged that the U-RANS approach may not fully capture the vortex propagation compared to a large eddy simulation approach, but they found a very significant matching between the numerical and experimental data.
The main challenges in accurately predicting the turbine performance at low tip-speed ratios were related to the severe flow separation and stall conditions experienced by the airfoils.
Additional factors like surface roughness and trailing-edge refinement can also play a significant role in the accurate prediction of the turbine performance at low tip-speed ratios.
The availability of reliable and detailed experimental data was pivotal for tuning the numerical tools and validating the CFD simulations.
The study aimed to correlate the main macrostructures of the flow with the unsteady aerodynamics of the airfoils in cycloidal motion.
